titleStmt.title: Data Science and Digital Art History
titleStmt.author: Лев Манович

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Data Science and Digital Art History

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: I present a number of core concepts from data science that are relevant to digital art history and the use of quantitative methods to study any cultural artifacts or processes in general.

span.label: computational analysis of large visual cultural datasets
span.quote: These concepts enable computational exploration of both large and small visual cultural data.

span.label: review
span.quote: These concepts do not require formulas to explain, and they can be presented in one article, which is what I will attempt here.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because a computer sees only low-level data (pixels, letters) and not meaning, analysts extract many additional features in the hope that together they carry enough information to bridge that gap.
span.quote: Trying to “close the semantic gap” (this is the standard phrase in computer science publications) is one of the motivations for using multiple features.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Human side-by-side comparison breaks down as collections grow, which is what forces the substitution of computed distance in feature space for perceptual comparison.
span.quote: Manual comparison does not scale well for big data.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The need to compute by hand constrained the founders of statistics to one- and two-variable methods, and that constraint still shapes how data is imagined today.
span.quote: The practicality of manual computation was an important consideration for the people who were consolidating statistics in the beginning of the 20th century.

span.label: The chosen examples are deliberately biased toward the humanities rather than being a neutral survey of data science.
span.note: what this limits: the choice of examples, declared as a specification rather than confessed: SINCE MY ARTICLE IS WRITTEN FOR HUMANITIES AUDIENCE, IT IS ON PURPOSE BIASED - MY EXAMPLES COME FROM HUMANITIES AS OPPOSED TO ECONOMICS OR SOCIOLOGY
span.quote: Since my article is written for humanities audience, it is on purpose biased–my examples of the application of the core concepts of data science come from humanities as opposed to economics or sociology.

span.label: A two-feature comparison of images ignores every other kind of difference between the works.
span.note: what this limits: the two-feature comparison: THIS EXAMPLE DISREGARDS ALL OTHER TYPES OF DIFFERENCE: SUBJECT MATTER, COMPOSITION, COLOR PALETTE, BRUSHWORK
span.quote: Note that, of course, this example disregards all other types of difference: subject matter, composition, color palette, brushwork, and so.

span.label: Even with many features there is no guarantee that the extracted features capture difference as humans perceive it.
span.note: what this limits: any feature-based measure of similarity: EVEN IF WE USE MANY DIFFERENT FEATURES, WE CANNOT BE SURE THAT WE HAVE CAPTURED THE RIGHT INFORMATION TO QUANTIFY DIFFERENCE AS WE HUMANS SEE IT
span.quote: Note that just as it was the case with van Gogh example, even if we use many different features, we cannot be sure that we have captured the right information to quantify difference as we humans see it.

span.label: Dimension-reduced plots are hard to interpret because the axes no longer correspond to single features.
span.note: what this limits: any reading of the reduced plots: IT CAN BE QUITE CHALLENGING TO INTERPRET THE MEANING OF EACH DIMENSION once dimension reduction has been applied
span.quote: This is the serious challenge of dimension reduction algorithms – while they allow us to represent data using scatterplots where we can see the structure of a space easily, it can be quite challenging to interpret the meaning of each dimension.

span.label: Computational analysis has a precondition that the article says cannot be changed: the phenomenon must first be made into a finite set of objects and a finite set of features.
span.note: what this limits: any computational result about a cultural phenomenon: the article states the phenomenon must first be represented as a finite set of individual objects and a finite set of their features
span.quote: Before we can use computers to analyze a phenomena or activity, it has to be represented as a finite set of individual objects and also a finite set of their features.

span.label: The comparison is confined to the chosen features, and everything else is set aside — which the article names as a limitation and then reframes as an advantage.
span.note: what this limits: a similarity computed over selected image features: the article states it disregards subject matter, composition, colour palette and brushwork, and treats that as both a limitation and an advantage
span.quote: this example disregards all other types of difference: subject matter, composition, color palette, brushwork, and so. However, this is not only a limitation

span.label: The demographic and facial variables in the featured project were produced by paid crowdworkers and a commercial face-analysis service.
span.note: what this limits: the age, gender and emotion variables in this project: the age and gender estimates came from Amazon Mechanical Turk and the facial features from a commercial recognition service
span.quote: Age and gender estimates were obtained by using Amazon Mechanical Turk service.

span.label: THE PAPER STATES THAT THE CENTRAL RISK CANNOT BE RETIRED BY ADDING MORE MEASUREMENT: 'even if we use many different features, WE CANNOT BE SURE THAT WE HAVE CAPTURED THE RIGHT INFORMATION to quantify difference as we humans see it'. It then declines the obvious repair - 'producing a single correct map should not be our main goal' - so the limitation is accepted as a condition of the method rather than treated as a defect to fix.
span.quote: Note that just as it was the case with van Gogh example, even if we use many different features, we cannot be sure that we have captured the right information to quantify difference as we humans see it

span.label: the core analytic concepts of data science (objects, features, feature space, distance, dimension reduction) are imported wholesale as a framework for art-historical and humanistic study
span.quote: I present a number of core concepts from data science that are relevant to digital art history and the use of quantitative methods to study any cultural artifacts or processes in general.

span.label: the term "features" is adopted into digital art history in place of the sciences' "variable", and stretched to cover existing metadata as well as computed attributes
span.quote: I suggest that in digital art history we adapt the term “features” to refer to both information that can be extracted from objects through computer analysis and the already available metadata.

span.label: data
span.quote: Before we can use computers to analyze a phenomena or activity, it has to be represented as a finite set of individual objects and also a finite set of their features.

span.label: phenomenon
span.quote: That is, a phenomenon is constituted by its representations and the conversations about it.

span.label: features
span.quote: but also an advantage – by letting us isolate particular features, we can compare artifacts only on dimensions we want.

span.label: objects
span.quote: But the concept of “data” also contains more basic and fundamental assumptions that cannot be changed, and 18 DAH-Journal, Issue 1, 2015 this is equally important. Before we can use computers to analyze a phenomena or activity, it has to be represented as a finite set

span.label: feature space
span.quote: To the concepts above (objects and features) we are going to add the third core concept: feature space. We assume that our data is stored in a table. But now we will conceptualize our data table as a geometric space of many dimensions. Each feature becomes one of the dimensions. Each object becomes a point in this space

span.label: phenomenon - AS INDEPENDENT: something that objectively exists regardless of how we study it, irrespective of which objects and properties we choose
span.quote: we could assume that a phenomenon (such as “contemporary society,” for example) objectively exists regardless of how we study it (i.e., what we use as objects and their properties).

span.label: phenomenon - AS CONSTITUTED: equal to the set of objects and properties used to study it, so that it is made by its representations and the conversations about it
span.quote: That is, a phenomenon is constituted by its representations and the conversations about it.

span.label: feature selection - stated as BOTH a limitation and an advantage, because isolating features is what makes comparison on chosen dimensions possible at all
span.quote: but also an advantage – by letting us isolate particular features, we can compare artifacts only on dimensions we want.

span.label: variable - used in opposite ways by the two fields the paper is joining: one isolated variable for understanding in statistics, many features for automation in data science
span.quote: Statistics and quantitative social science that uses it ideally wants to isolate one independent and one dependent variable, because the goal is understanding the phenomenon. Data science wants to use many features in the hope that together they contain the right information for automating recognition, classification, or another cognitive task

span.label: extends → Franco Moretti, 'Conjectures on World Literature' (2000)
span.quote: Moretti’s point certainly applies to all other humanities fields; and it applies even more to the analysis of contemporary culture.

span.label: phenomenon —operationalised-as→ objects
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE PRECONDITION THE PAPER SAYS CANNOT BE CHANGED: 'Before we can use computers to analyze a phenomena or activity, IT HAS TO BE REPRESENTED AS A FINITE SET of individual objects and also a finite set' of features. The record already carries the two readings of `phenomenon` as senses - AS INDEPENDENT, existing regardless of description, and AS CONSTITUTED, equal to the objects and properties chosen. This edge is the move between them, and the paper marks it as an ASSUMPTION that is fundamental and unalterable rather than as a step in a method.
span.quote: But the concept of “data” also contains more basic and fundamental assumptions that cannot be changed, and 18 DAH-Journal, Issue 1, 2015 this is equally important. Before we can use computers to analyze a phenomena or activity, it has to be represented as a finite set

span.label: features —operationalised-as→ feature space
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — The second constituting move, stated as a conceptualisation rather than a discovery: 'we will CONCEPTUALIZE our data table as a geometric space of many dimensions. Each feature becomes one of the dimensions. Each object becomes a point in this space.' Similarity becomes distance because the table is read as a space.
span.quote: To the concepts above (objects and features) we are going to add the third core concept: feature space. We assume that our data is stored in a table. But now we will conceptualize our data table as a geometric space of many dimensions. Each feature becomes one of the dimensions. Each object becomes a point in this space

span.label: features —contrasted-with→ data
span.note: differs in: WHAT MANY VARIABLES ARE FOR, and the two fields use them in opposite ways: statistics 'ideally wants to ISOLATE ONE independent and one dependent variable, BECAUSE THE GOAL IS UNDERSTANDING the phenomenon', while data science 'wants to use MANY features in the hope that together they contain the right information for AUTOMATING recognition, classification'. Understanding and automating pull the design of the measurement apart · strength of the relation: 0.8
span.quote: Statistics and quantitative social science that uses it ideally wants to isolate one independent and one dependent variable, because the goal is understanding the phenomenon. Data science wants to use many features in the hope that together they contain the right information for automating recognition, classification, or another cognitive task

span.label: principal component analysis
span.quote: We then used Principal Component Analysis to reduce the space of 200 features to a smaller number of dimensions, and visualized the first two dimensions.

span.label: multidimensional scaling
span.quote: Figure 5: Visualization of the data from Fig. 4 using multi-dimensional Scaling (MDS).

span.label: mean
span.quote: In each visualization, images are organized by mean hue (angle) and brightness mean (distance to the center).

span.label: Classical statistics and data science use variables in opposite ways: statistics isolates one independent and one dependent variable in order to explain a phenomenon, while data science piles up many features in order to automate a cognitive task.
span.quote: Statistics and quantitative social science that uses it ideally wants to isolate one independent and one dependent variable, because the goal is understanding the phenomenon. Data science wants to use many features in the hope that together they contain the right information for automating recognition, classification, or another cognitive task.

span.label: The feature-space concept lets the humanities' oldest method, comparison, be scaled up to very large cultural datasets.
span.quote: The concept of a geometric feature space allows us to take the most basic method of humanities – a comparison – and extend it to big cultural data.

span.label: Representing images as points in a feature space converts visual difference into geometric distance, which is what makes machine comparison of millions of images possible.
span.quote: In such representation, the visual difference between images is equated with a distance in feature space.

span.label: Automatic classification, the single most common application of data science, is the least valuable one for the humanities, which should instead use computation to question existing categories.
span.quote: Among the contemporary applications of data science, probably the most common is automatic classification. However, in my view it is the least interesting one for humanities.

span.label: Dimension reduction makes the shape of a high-dimensional space visible but at the cost of interpretability, because each plotted axis stands for a combination of features rather than one feature.
span.quote: This is the serious challenge of dimension reduction algorithms – while they allow us to represent data using scatterplots where we can see the structure of a space easily, it can be quite challenging to interpret the meaning of each dimension.

span.label: Plotted on average brightness and average saturation, van Gogh's Paris paintings spread more widely than his Arles paintings, most of which occupy the same region as the Paris works.
span.quote: The visualization shows that on these dimensions, van Gogh’s Paris paintings have more variability than his Arles paintings.

span.label: In a PCA map of roughly 6000 Impressionist paintings, the bright canvases the public associates with Impressionism are a minority; at least half of the works are darker and closer to conventional nineteenth-century painting.
span.quote: One interesting finding is that the types of images popularly associated with Impressionism (lower left part) constitute only a smaller part of the larger set of artworks created by these artists.

span.label: Instagram tags from the 2014 Kyiv Maidan protests split into two barely-connected clusters, generic global Instagram tags and locally specific event tags, indicating two separate user populations.
span.quote: The visualization suggests that there is little interaction between these two types of tags: one group of Instagram users was using generic tags while another group was primarily tagging the local and specific events.

span.label: data science
span.quote: Data science includes classical statistical techniques from the 19th and early 20th century, additional techniques and concepts for data analysis that were developed starting in 1960s with the help of computers, and concepts from a number fields that also develop in the second part of the 20th century around computers: pattern recognition, information retrieval, artificial intelligence, computer science, machine learning, information visualization, data mining.

span.label: features (as redefined for digital art history)
span.term: features (as redefined for digital art history)
span.quote: I suggest that in digital art history we adapt the term “features” to refer to both information that can be extracted from objects through computer analysis and the already available metadata.

span.label: data / dataset
span.quote: Together, the objects and their features is what we mean by "data" (or "datasets").

span.label: feature space
span.quote: Each feature becomes one of the dimensions. Each object becomes a point in this space.

span.label: dimension reduction
span.quote: It refers to various algorithms that create a low dimension representation of a multi-dimensional space.

span.label: semantic gap
span.quote: This is the gap between knowledge that a human being can extract from some data, and how computer sees the same data.

span.label: coding (manual description of data in social science)
span.term: coding (manual description of data in social science)
span.quote: In social science, the process of manually adding descriptions of data is called coding.

span.label: supervised learning
span.quote: In contrast, "supervised learning" needs part of the data already labeled as belonging to this or that category.

span.label: average color saturation and average hue of an image
span.term: average color saturation and average hue of an image
span.quote: 50,000 Instagram images shared in Bangkok are compared with 50,000 Instagram images shared in Tokyo using two features extracted by computer analysis – average color saturation, and average hue.

span.label: city in which the Instagram image was shared (Bangkok vs. Tokyo)
span.term: city in which the Instagram image was shared (Bangkok vs. Tokyo)
span.quote: 50,000 Instagram images shared in Bangkok are compared with 50,000 Instagram images shared in Tokyo using two features extracted by computer analysis – average color saturation, and average hue.

span.label: 10.5 million — number of publicly visible Instagram images collected across New York City over five months in 2014 for the On Broadway project
span.quote: The result was 10.5 million images.

span.label: 6,165 / 13,208 / 21,465 (5845 unique) — Instagram users, images and tags (and unique tags) collected in central Kyiv over 17–22 February 2014
span.quote: During this period 6,165 Instagram users shared 13,208 images which they tagged with the total of 21,465 tags (5845 unique tags).

span.label: 200 — number of visual features the lab extracted from each Impressionist painting image before reducing dimensions
span.quote: We extracted 200 separate features from each image, describing its color characteristics, contrast, shapes, textures and some aspects of composition.

span.label: approximately 6000 — size of the French Impressionist painting dataset visualised with PCA
span.quote: The data set is digital images of approximately 6000 paintings by French Impressionists.

span.label: 3200 — number of Instagram self-portraits assembled and made filterable in the Selfiecity interface
span.quote: A visitor can filter the collection of 3200 Instagram self-portraits by using graphs in the upper part of the screen.

span.label: 50,000 — size of the random Instagram image sample taken from each of Bangkok and Tokyo for the Phototrails comparison
span.quote: Left: a random sample of 50,000 Instagram images from Bangkok. Right: a random sample of 50,000 Instagram images from Tokyo.
